Sure.
Well, thanks for having me, Leandro.

As you mentioned, my name's Jeremy Kokomor.
I started a firm called right-tail capital about three years ago, and basically, I manage

I like to own the businesses for several years at a time, partly because I believe that it's

I'm based in the U.S., all my clients have a separately managed account, and it's really

Speaking about alignment, I think your right-tail capital is unconventional in its fee structure.
The normal fee structure in the industry is, you see nowadays, it's a management fee
followed by a performance fee, and the management fee tends to oscillate between 1% and 2%.
But you have a different fee structure that actually is quite rare today and aligns your

What do you speak a bit about that?
Sure.
I thought about trying to create alignment in several different ways.
The fee structure, as you mentioned, is one of the ways, and I'm a big Warren Buffett
fan, have been for a long time, and I was always very drawn to his original fee structure
when he was managing the Buffett partnerships many, many decades ago before Berkshire Hathaway.
The fee structure he used was a 0% management fee, and then a performance fee that was nothing
for the first 6% of returns, and then 25% of any returns over 6%.
So I thought that would be one way to create alignment with my investors, and that performance
fee structure is one of the fee structures I've chosen.
Now I do also have a management fee structure primarily just to give investors a choice
and to pick the one that resonates most with them.
But that's kind of the overall framework of the performance fee structure.
How have you found any difference between customer choosing one or the other?
Why do you think there are one customer may choose one or the other?
Sure.
On your second question, I think it boils down to, we all have different preferences when
it comes to money and investing.
Morgan Housel talks about this a lot, and is also booked the psychology of money.
This can be due to our whole lives of just what did our grandparents teach us about
money, and what did our parents teach us about money, and what did our personal circumstances
expose us to?
One thing that has surprised me is that roughly half of my investors have chosen each fee structure.
And also my ability to predict what someone might choose has been very, very low.
So ultimately, I think it just comes down to what resonates the most with someone.
So I'm happy that there are some choices for each person to think through.
Let's talk about the name right-tail capital, because I think it's interesting because it
captures what any investor should strive to do, which is to capture the right-tail of
investments.
I mean, one of the best things about investing in equities is that the upside is technically
unlimited, and then your downside is limited.
So obviously, long-term returns have been skewed to the right-tail of the distribution.
So what characteristics do you believe a right-tail investment needs to have?
Sure, well, you hit the nail on the head.
The name right-tail really had certain different meanings for me.
First and foremost, I want our long-term returns just over many years to be in a right-tail
and to be excellent.
Secondly, I'm typically going to be investing in higher-quality businesses that have proven
themselves to be in a right-tail, both versus company in their industry, and then also
relative to companies at large.
And then lastly, when I think about right-tail, there are also some personal meanings for
me, which is we all know that small improvements applied consistently can really add up over time.
That's the whole concept of compounding is what may sound like pretty basic numbers
in one year.
If you apply it over a really long period of time, those returns or those improvements
can really add up to something really, really fantastic over a longer period of time.
And so on a personal level, I love the process of how do we all get a little bit better
each day, whether it's related to investing or fitness, or just general knowledge.
So there are several reasons that the name right-tail really resonated with me.
In terms of a right-tail investment, it would be putting some of those factors together.
So I want to have an investment that has the opportunity to generate outstanding returns
over many years.
For me, what I'm typically looking for is an investment that I think can double in five
years or less, which would equate to a 15% IRR or higher.
And in terms of how I get there, I usually want to find high-quality businesses that I believe
I can pay a fair to the low average price for.
And you talked there about the term compounding, and you also talked about quality.
I think the term compounder probably, I think it's what any investor should strive to achieve.
But at the same time, it's probably a term that has been thrown out there, maybe too much,
especially in recent times.
I think the term is also related to linear compounders, right?
A lot of people, when they think about compounders, they think about companies that only
or stocks that only go up, can a cyclical company feed your quality mold?
Absolutely, absolutely.
You know, I tend to think that most businesses, as well as most things in life,
are rarely perfectly linear.
In fact, I have not heard that I could think of something that kind of fits that mold.
The world is an uncertain place, and even a lot of great businesses that have produced
outstanding investment returns over time, will typically have, at a minimum, some stock
price volatility at some point.
Maybe it's a slowdown in the business or some perceptions whether real or perceived
that the business is going through a tougher period that can create some volatility.
In a similar way, cyclical businesses can absolutely be compounders, and sometimes going
through a more challenging part in the cycle can actually create a better buying opportunity.
In a couple of different ways, one way, maybe the one that is most obvious is just a reduced
price that allows us to buy a very good business at a very reasonable valuation, maybe even
on earnings that are slightly or even more so depressed.
So that's one way, another piece that I think about a lot, and one reason I really like
to invest in higher quality businesses, is that I know when a business inevitably hits
a rough path, whether it is this challenging part of the cycle or something else, a higher
quality business, a higher quality management team, often that comes with a better balance
sheet as well.
All of these factors should allow that business to use the cycle to their advantage and
potentially come out of the other side of that cycle as an even stronger business,
maybe one that has gained market share or gained additional loyalty from their customers.
So for all these reasons, we can absolutely find great businesses that can compound as
an investment, even if they are cyclical.
I think the business that comes closest, in terms of the stock performance to linear
compounding, that I can think of is probably Constellation Software.
I think, well, it has compounded at a 30% rate since 2006, and I think it has never been
more than 30% of highs, which is outstanding, right?
I mean, even the market has been down more than 30% several times in the last years.
But that's probably the only one that I can think of from the top of my head.
And we're now going to go into the conversation as such.
And I think this question was a very good introduction of finding quality where you least
expect it to, right?
So that's going to be the topic of today's episode.
This topic always brings me back to a chart shared by Michael Mabuzan, where he shows
that he shows the ROIC on average cost of capital differential for many industries.
And you can clearly see that there are industries that are more prone to value creation, right?
He shares, you can clearly spot them out in the chart.
And I think this is where a lot of people look for quality companies, right?
Because if you're looking in a pond where adding value is, let's say, relatively easy,
then it's tougher to be, it's tough to be wrong, right?
But what I think that was the goal of the chart.
But what I got from it was that in certain industries where adding value is tough or where
the industry in general destroyed value, there were certain companies that managed to consistently
add value.
So what the conclusion here is that you can find quality everywhere, right?
And some places it's more likely, in some places it's less.
The good news of looking where nobody is looking is that maybe you find more interesting
valuations.
So for example, if you're looking at a pond or an industry where typically value has been
destroyed, then it might be easier to find mispricings.
So I know Jeremy that you own several companies that can, that might not be considered quality,
let's say by the quality as our term that we hear today, like linear compounders in super
strong industries.
So let's talk about some of those and why they have performed so well.
So if you want to, you can share a couple of businesses that maybe feel that feel fit this
mold of a quality company that's maybe not considered as such.
Sure.
Well, you know, you just shared a lot of awesome insights and, you know, I agree with what

And I try to understand businesses and industries, you know, regardless of what they look like

And so, you know, I do own a company like Constellation Software, which kind of fits the bucket

So if you that I'll mention briefly and then we can, we can dive into them in more detail

And in one of the companies that has always jumped out to me and I've been an investor

States.
However, for several reasons, they look very different than what most, and they do some things

So I started industry that, you know, I've had a lot of fun exploring over the past few

And I respect several companies in that industry as an industry that is extremely fragmented

So let's talk first about NVR.
So what is the, I think the name is a bit confusing, right?
Because home building, home builders actually don't build homes generally.
So what do home builders do and why is it an attractive industry in the U.S.?
Sure.
Well, historically, what the home building industry has done is, you know, buy and develop
raw parcels of land and then take that raw piece of land through the whole process of,
you know, developing the land, getting it permitted, and then actually building the home on
the land and selling it to a customer.
So historically, that is what the industry has been focused on.
Now NVR around 30 years ago went through a really challenging period coming out of the
savings and loan crisis where they had owned too much land.
The business actually almost went bankrupt.
And so the management team decided, you know, hey, this model isn't working for us.
And so they pivoted to a business model where they very, very rarely own and develop the
land that they built homes on.
Instead, they will work out, you know, they will, they will purchase an option from the
land developer to build a home on that piece of land.
And the reason for that is that they felt that the land ownership was the riskiest part
of the process.
Yes, it can produce good returns when done well and when in, you know, kind of a normal
part of the cycle.
But the land ownership piece, when you go through a really challenging part of the cycle,
it's super liquid, it's probably worth less than what you thought it was worth.
And so that can get businesses and a lot of trouble when you go through a really challenging
period, like the savings of the loan crisis or like the great financial crisis in 2008.
And even if it's a good period, you get a lot of capital tied into that land, right?
So the capital efficiency is not the best.
Absolutely, absolutely.
And I think, you know, I think the counterpoint to that is the companies that do own land
will say, well, yes, we can produce a higher growth margin by developing that land ourselves.
I think that misses the broader point that you just made of the capital efficiency being
more difficult.
And, you know, studying NDR reminds me of a quote that Bucket has made over the years.
You know, is that when, you know, you're looking at the low cost provider in an industry,
you know, I think our natural inclination as humans is to kind of say, oh, okay, yeah,
these are two companies in the same industry once a little bit better than the other.
And Buffett kind of reminds us, you know, no, actually that that low cost producer provided
that they have a sustainable competitive advantage is actually, you know, a much different business
and we should think of it as maybe, you know, being in a completely different industry
altogether because it is so much different and better than a lot of its competitors.
No, absolutely.
And one thing that surprises me about the home building industry is that MVR is doing this for quite a long time,
100% options on the land.
But then many other competitors have also other home builders have also jumped into
optioning land, but they are very, they are skeptics on going on a 100% optioning model, right?
Despite what they've seen that that MVR has managed to do, right? And obviously,
I imagine that there are barriers to entry to go to that model because then you also have,

So why do you think that what MVR has been doing has been sustainable?
Let's say, why do you think, what do you think keeps other home builders away from the same model?
It's a great question. And, you know, I think it boils down to a couple of different things.
You know, one is home building is an industry where there are some benefits to scale.
One of them in particular is just that if you are a bigger company, you probably have better
access to financing than, you know, kind of your very small home builder that is just in one
market and builds like 10 or even 100 homes per year. And so since there are some advantages
to being larger, I think that creates an environment where, you know, the bigger companies should be,
you know, better set up to succeed over time. And the bigger companies historically
have developed their own land. And so your question, your question gets to a great point about,

you know, probably makes sense on paper, you know, makes sense if you're, you know, a business school

But companies are, you know, kind of living organisms with their own culture and many years of experience.
And so to go, to go, you know, from a, from a position where you own and develop all of your land

of the staff that you would have to, you know, cut to do something like that, which I don't think

a company like NVR has, has built over the years. And so those are a couple of reasons that I think
it's a harder model to copy than, you know, what might just kind of jump out to us immediately.

And I remember I quote by Dream Finder Somes CEO, who said that when it comes to land options,

we will see what happens if a new real estate crisis comes our way and see how the business

thing that also is interesting about NVR is that they are very, let's say out of the spotlight,

or do you think it's irrelevant? I mean, good in the sense that maybe the management team

You know, I think it aligns with how they run their business. You know, in terms of
